author: DailyMail
title: Furious Residents as Travellers Smash Through Gate to Set Up Illegal Encampment
text:
Residents of a leafy suburb have been left furious after travellers smashed through a gate to pitch up an illegal encampment on their local recreational park. The group used bolt cutters and angle grinders to smash through a lock and gain access on Monday afternoon. The site provides the main entrance to Birmingham's Woodgate Valley Country Park, a 450-acre beauty spot home to rivers, meadows and scenic walkways. However, the encampment has rendered that haven nearly inaccessible. Local residents are now fearing a repeat of the mess left behind by the travellers last time they set up camp.
Residents of a leafy suburb have been left furious after travellers smashed through a gate to pitch up an illegal encampment on their local recreational park.
The group used bolt cutters and angle grinders to smash through a lock and gain access on Monday afternoon. The site provides the main entrance to Birmingham's Woodgate Valley Country Park, a 450-acre beauty spot home to rivers, meadows and scenic walkways.
However, the encampment has rendered that haven nearly inaccessible. Local residents are now fearing a repeat of the mess left behind by the travellers last time they set up camp. The group left behind bags of rubbish, toiletries, dirty nappies, and human and dog excrement. The area is heavily used by dog walkers, nature lovers, and kids, and the travellers' destruction of the grassland and the waste they leave behind is a major concern.
The arrival of the travellers comes just five days before a dozen tip trucks were set to visit Highfield Lane to pick up household rubbish, garden waste, and recycling. The scheme was set up by Birmingham City Council in a bid to tackle fly-tipping in Britain's second city, which reached a point of crisis last year amid bin shortages. Residents had been awaiting the visit for weeks, but now fear it could be cancelled due to the illegal encampment.
The travellers' arrival has also sparked concerns about the increasing number of unauthorised encampments in the city. Last month alone, reports suggest that as many as seven illegal encampments were pitched up across Birmingham. It came after council data revealed officers in the city dealt with 132 unauthorised encampments involving 2,280 caravans in 2025-26. That represented a 43 per cent and 75 per cent increase respectively from the previous year's 92 encampments and 1,308 caravans.
The increasing number of travellers in the area has left residents feeling frustrated and concerned about their safety and the state of the local environment. The travellers' destruction of the grassland and the waste they leave behind is a major concern for local residents, who are worried about the impact on the local ecosystem and the health and well-being of their children.
The situation has sparked a heated debate about the need for more effective measures to tackle the problem of travellers in the city. Some residents are calling for the council to take a tougher stance on travellers, while others are advocating for more support and resources to be provided to help them find alternative accommodation.
The council has announced plans to tackle the issue, but it remains to be seen whether these measures will be effective in reducing the number of unauthorised encampments in the city. In the meantime, residents are left to deal with the consequences of the travellers' actions, including the destruction of the grassland and the waste they leave behind. The situation has left many feeling frustrated, concerned, and fearful for the future of their community.
